# Dawes and Young Plans (1924-1930)

 Version 2.0 Latest review activity 30 July 2026 Review clock starts 30 July 2026 Editorially checked All rights reserved

The Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929-1930) were creditor-engineered restructurings of German reparations that wound down the coercive phase of the reparations conflict, replacing enforcement by occupation with stabilisation by American capital. Together they mark the transition from reparations as continued economic war to reparations as a managed, and ultimately unpayable, financial workout.

## Context

The Ruhr occupation of 1923 and the German hyperinflation demonstrated that extraction by force destroyed the capacity it sought to tax. The Dawes committee of experts, chaired by the American banker Charles G. Dawes, was convened to make payment technically feasible without adjudicating the total owed.

## Campaign

The Dawes Plan (in force September 1924) restarted payments on a rising annuity scale, beginning at one billion gold marks and reaching two and a half billion after five years, stabilised the currency, and secured payments on German railways and industry. Its two load-bearing features were an 800 million gold mark international loan, floated substantially on Wall Street, and transfer protection: reparations could be suspended in transfer if they endangered the mark, shifting exchange risk to the creditors. French and Belgian troops left the Ruhr in 1925, the evacuation completing in August. The Young Plan, negotiated in 1929 under Owen D. Young and effective in 1930, made the settlement notionally final: a 59-year annuity schedule whose payments, including interest, totalled about 112 billion gold marks on a principal of 36 billion, the end of foreign controls over German finances, and the creation of the Bank for International Settlements to administer transfers.

## Outcome

The architecture rested on circular capital flow, American lending to Germany funding reparations to the Allies funding war-debt payments to America, and it failed with the flow. The 1931 financial crisis brought the Hoover Moratorium, and the Lausanne Conference of 1932 ended reparations in all but name. Schuker's provocative calculation that net capital movement made the arrangement an "American reparations to Germany" is contested but captures the direction of funds after 1924.

## Assessment

The plans are the standard case of de-escalation in economic warfare: coercion abandoned not from generosity but because it was self-defeating, with private capital markets substituted for bayonets as the enforcement mechanism, and failing in their turn.
